Boeing/Airbus production delays impacting OEM aerospace revenue
FX headwinds from dollar strength affecting European and Asian revenues
Working capital pressure from seasonal Q1 patterns
margin_factors: Gross margin recovery to 37.3% from Q4's depressed 35.5% - cost actions gaining traction

SG&A discipline as breakup preparation drives operational efficiency

forecasts.thesis: My differentiated view is that Wall Street consensus of $2.31 EPS meaningfully underestimates the Q1 2026 earnings impact from the confirmed high-single-digit percentage revenue headwind due to Middle East shipping delays. I model this as a ~7.06% (~$693M) revenue decline versus Q1 2025, coupled with ~170 bps of gross margin compression from volume deleverage and an unfavorable product mix shift. Furthermore, consensus appears to overlook the normalization of non-operating income from Q4's anomalous $552M gain to a projected ~$150M loss, contributing an additional ~$0.11 EPS headwind. The key data points are management's explicit quantification of the revenue delay and the historical sensitivity of margins to volume. My forecast of $2.22 EPS represents a -3.9% miss versus consensus. I would change my mind if real-time shipping data showed a faster-than-expected resolution to the geopolitical disruptions or if preliminary segment results indicated stronger pricing power than modeled.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1’26 view remains modest-below-consensus on EPS ($2.28 vs $2.31) because the Street is likely smoothing through the disruption-driven timing hit and underweighting the near-term absorption and below-the-line drag from separation/financing actions. Even if management maintains full-year guidance, Q1 is the quarter where timing and fixed-cost absorption can matter most, and tender/financing activity increases the chance that interest/transaction noise shows up in reported results.

I’m modeling revenue of $9.25B (down ~6% YoY vs Q1’25’s $9.82B), consistent with management’s characterization of a high-single-digit Q1 disruption impact, with partial catch-up before quarter end. Mix (Aerospace/service) and cost discipline keep operating profit resilient, but not enough to fully offset under-absorption and higher net interest expense. I would change my view if evidence emerges that shipments deferred early in the quarter are largely recovered within Q1 (raising both revenue and margin), or if disclosed separation/financing costs are materially lighter than assumed.

Separation/financing transaction costs land in Q1 more heavily than anticipated (EPS downside)
FX and tax-rate volatility could swing below-the-line results
margin_factors: Under-absorption from lower volume partially offset by favorable mix (Aero/service) and productivity
OpEx discipline (SG&A pacing) offsets incremental separation-related overhead
Net interest expense elevated due to financing actions/tender activity and higher run-rate debt cost

Aerospace OE + aftermarket resilience: offsets a portion of disruption-driven timing
Industrial Automation: stable-to-soft macro and project timing keeps growth muted
Building Automation & Energy/Sustainability: steadier service/software mix provides ballast

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of -$0.17 for HOVR represents a 29% beat versus the Street's -$0.24 consensus, driven by three structural factors Wall Street is systematically mispricing. First, the normalized operating expense trajectory shows clear sequential improvement: Q1's $5.9M OpEx included ~$1.2M of non-recurring G&A items (elevated professional fees, one-time compensation accruals), Q2 normalized to $5.1M, and I project $4.5M for Q3 as G&A continues declining toward the $2.0M run-rate management is targeting. This alone accounts for ~$0.03 of my beat vs consensus. Second, non-operating losses are moderating: the $5.0M Q1 and $3.5M Q2 warrant mark-to-market losses reflected extreme stock volatility during the initial trading period post-SPAC, but price action has stabilized and I model $2.4M for Q3 - still elevated but normalizing.

The key insight the Street is missing is that they're extrapolating from abnormally elevated Q1 losses without adjusting for the non-recurring expense items and the mean-reversion in warrant volatility. HOVR's core business - pre-revenue hybrid eVTOL development - actually shows disciplined execution. The March 15 Cavorite X7 technical update confirms development is proceeding on schedule with no evidence of cost overruns. Cash position is strong: I project ~$30.5M by Q3 end (up from $24.3M Q2) providing 12+ months runway at current burn rates. The 10-Q filings confirm no near-term liquidity concerns.

What would change my view: (1) If warrant liability losses exceed $3.5M due to renewed stock volatility, my estimate could miss by $0.03-0.04; (2) If development hits unexpected technical challenges requiring accelerated R&D spending; (3) If G&A doesn't normalize as expected due to ongoing public company costs. My conviction is medium - this is a speculative pre-revenue company with inherent unpredictability, but the Street's -$0.24 consensus appears to be mechanically rolling forward elevated Q1 losses without proper normalization.

The underlying business fundamentals remain solid with Software segment expected to grow +9.5% YoY on watsonx and Red Hat momentum, validated by the ElevenLabs integration announcement for enterprise-grade agentic AI voice capabilities.

Infrastructure remains in pre-z17 cycle trough at -3% YoY, which is fully expected and should not surprise. The Q4 2025 10-K filing and subsequent 8-K filings provide clean data on segment performance but limited new forward guidance beyond management's prior commentary.

Conversely, I would lower estimates if macro deterioration accelerates consulting pullback or if tax rate normalizes higher than 17%. The mechanical 'consensus' of -$0.20 is not a true analyst estimate but rather a distorted four-quarter average that inappropriately weights Q1 2025's merger-related gains (EPS of +$0.10) and other non-recurring items. IsoEnergy's normalized operating profile shows quarterly G&A running in the $4-5M range, and with the February 2026 equity raise significantly bolstering the cash position to approximately $162M in liquid assets, interest income should reach approximately $1.6M for the quarter - a material offset to operating expenses.

The key differentiation in my view versus the mechanical consensus is understanding that IsoEnergy is a pre-revenue exploration company with a predictable cost structure. Q4 2025's elevated G&A of $6.4M included one-time items that should not repeat in Q1 2026. With Tony M bulk sampling commenced in January 2026 and the restart decision expected in H2 2026, near-term operational activities are focused on sample processing and analysis rather than major new capital deployments. The company's strong cash position post-equity raise provides substantial runway and interest income that the distorted consensus fails to capture.

The Murphy Lake geophysics news from UraniumX confirms continued regional exploration interest near IsoEnergy's Hurricane deposit but has no direct financial impact on Q1 2026 results. The broader uranium sector sentiment remains bullish as evidenced by the March 15, 2026 reporting on IsoEnergy gaining traction amid nuclear energy demand surge. However, this positive sentiment is a longer-term driver for valuation rather than a near-term earnings catalyst. My conviction remains medium given the inherent uncertainty around exploration-stage companies and potential for unexpected non-cash charges or timing differences in expense recognition.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $5.18 remains 4.4% below the Street consensus of $5.42, reflecting a more conservative but slightly improved stance from my prior $5.15 estimate. The modest upward revision is driven by March news flow showing continued institutional appetite for financial sector exposure (Westview's $3.39M JPM position initiation) and JPMorgan's active role hosting corporate events like the Home Depot presentation, which signals sustained deal pipeline activity. However, I maintain my below-consensus view because the Street appears to be extrapolating Q4 2025's exceptional trading quarter ($9.8B in markets revenue) into Q1 without adequately accounting for typical seasonal normalization.

The key tension in my model is between management's bullish February commentary about 'jumping deal fees and trading revenue' and the fundamental headwinds from Fed rate cuts flowing through the asset side faster than liabilities reprice. I'm modeling NII at $24.4B versus Q4's $25.0B, representing a 2.4% sequential decline that I believe consensus is underweighting. Trading revenue at $9.3B represents a 5% QoQ decline from Q4's peak, which I view as conservative given historical Q1 seasonality. The IB pipeline at $2.7B is a bright spot, up from $2.3B in Q4, supported by management guidance and active capital markets conditions.

What would change my view: If March trading desk performance data suggests volatility remained elevated (currently appears lower), I would consider revising upward. Conversely, if Q1 deposit flows show accelerated migration to higher-yielding products, NII compression could be worse than my $24.4B estimate. The Street's $5.42 consensus implies approximately $15.1B in net income and a 20%+ ROTCE - achievable but optimistic given the mixed macro backdrop and Q4's elevated comparison base.

My Q1 2026 EPS forecast ($5.51) is slightly above the Street ($5.42), but with tighter upside than my prior $5.58 because Q1 seasonality typically keeps expenses sticky and the precise magnitude/timing of the CIB fee uplift is hard to handicap without fresh deal/tape data. The core differentiated call is that consensus is likely over-anchored to NII pressure while underweighting the probability-weighted rebound in CIB (Markets + IB fees) and a cleaner credit-cost setup versus a quarter with discrete reserve actions.

The key setup is visible in the recent earnings pattern: firm revenue has held near ~$69–72B across the last four quarters while EPS swung meaningfully (Q4 2025 EPS $4.63 vs $5.07–$5.09 prior), implying credit/markets and expense mix drive large incremental EPS. I’m modeling Q1 revenue at ~$72.8B with operating income ~$20.2B and an effective tax that yields ~$15.3B net income, translating to ~$5.51 EPS on ~2.78B shares.

I would change my mind (downside) if March markets activity was materially weaker than expected or if management takes a more conservative provisioning stance (e.g., broad-based reserve build). Upside would come from a sharper-than-modeled investment banking fee conversion and stronger trading, with stable credit costs.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $8.82 represents a modest upward revision from my prior $8.78 forecast, maintaining my strong variant view that the stated consensus of $0.51 is fundamentally erroneous. Karooooo has consistently delivered EPS in the $7.83-$9.48 range over the past five quarters with remarkable stability, making a sub-$1 consensus figure implausible - the true consensus among informed analysts tracking this stock likely sits in the $8.50-$9.00 range. My revenue projection of $1.45B represents a continuation of the highly consistent ~4% QoQ growth pattern ($1.23B → $1.28B → $1.34B → $1.39B), supported by ongoing fleet management adoption in African and Asian emerging markets.

The key analytical question remains whether Q3's SG&A surge to $546M from $487M in Q2 represents a structural shift or timing-driven investment volatility. I project partial normalization to $525M - above the Q2 level but below the Q3 spike - reflecting that some marketing and expansion investments were likely front-loaded while others represent ongoing growth investments. This assumption drives my operating income projection of $412M, above Q3's $358.8M which was compressed by the SG&A spike. The gross margin is projected to hold at ~69%, consistent with the improving trend from 71.2% in Q4 2025 adjusted for higher hardware costs as subscriber base expands.

What could prove me wrong: (1) If SG&A remains at $546M+ levels, indicating these are structural investments rather than timing-driven, EPS could come in closer to $8.30-8.50; (2) ZAR currency volatility has historically caused significant swings (the Q4 2025 forex effect was +$164.8M on cash flow) and could impact reported results materially in either direction; (3) If subscriber growth decelerates below the 4% QoQ trend, revenue would disappoint. The recent Wall Street Zen downgrade appears valuation-driven rather than fundamental-driven, and new director/insider filings (Leong, Ong) are standard housekeeping with no signal value.

However, the Q2 print should demonstrate management's ability to adapt to the new CA wage environment. If gross margin comes in below 9.5%, I would reassess my FY2026 outlook significantly. The stock's 37% institutional ownership reduction (Granite Partners) and insider selling suggest some near-term skepticism, but this appears more valuation-related than fundamental.

I’d change my mind toward breakeven EPS if evidence emerges (or the print shows) that restaurant-level margins normalized much faster—e.g., costOfRevenue closer to ~87–88% of sales—because incremental gross profit would flow quickly given a largely fixed SG&A base. Conversely, if KRUS repeats Q1-level cost ratios, EPS downside is meaningful even with revenue above $70M.

My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 is 1.25% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $1.60, reflecting conviction that the Street is still underweighting North American irrigation headwinds during what should be the company's peak seasonal quarter. CNH's Q4 2025 confirmation of 15-20% agricultural equipment demand declines and active dealer destocking provides critical cross-reference evidence that farmers are deferring capital equipment purchases. The comparison against Q2 2025's exceptional $187M/$2.44 quarter makes this particularly visible - I project revenue of $167.5M representing a -10.5% YoY decline.

However, I am revising my estimate modestly upward from $1.57 to $1.58 based on stronger Infrastructure segment momentum than previously modeled. Federal Signal's record Q4 2025 results (27% net sales growth, record orders) confirms infrastructure spending tailwinds are robust and accelerating. Lindsay's Road Runner TMA has now been in the commercial market for 5+ weeks, providing sufficient time for meaningful order contribution. I now model Infrastructure +18% YoY vs my prior +15% assumption, contributing approximately $1M incremental revenue and $0.01 EPS uplift.

The key swing factor remains the magnitude of North American irrigation weakness. If dealer destocking proves less severe than CNH's commentary suggests (perhaps -5% instead of -10%), there could be $0.05+ EPS upside to my estimate. Conversely, if Farm Belt spending deteriorates further or international markets weaken on FX, there's similar downside. I maintain medium conviction given the offsetting dynamics between weak irrigation and strong infrastructure.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast maintains the -$0.15 EPS estimate (approximately KRW -266B net loss), representing a material divergence from the implied Street consensus of +$0.18 EPS. The fundamental disconnect driving my variant view is that Wall Street appears to be modeling off operating income improvements without properly accounting for the substantial non-operating cost structure. While LG Display achieved positive operating income for two consecutive quarters (KRW 431B Q3, KRW 169B Q4 2025), the KRW 12.7T debt burden creates ~KRW 155B quarterly interest expense, and total non-operating drag consistently runs KRW 400-540B per quarter from interest, FX losses, and other financial costs. This structural drag mathematically prevents positive EPS even with modest operating profits.

Today's news flow reinforces my bearish thesis. The March 26 headline explicitly cites 'persistent industry oversupply in the display panel market and softening demand for OLED panels' - this validates my assumption of pricing pressure and volume headwinds. The March 25 news confirms 'inventory buildups at major clients like Apple and Samsung' which directly impacts the mobile/IT OLED segment representing ~45% of revenue. While the 1Hz LCD panel launch with Dell is technologically impressive (48% battery improvement), mass production just commenced, meaning Q1 contribution is negligible. The IP litigation win against Tianma is a medium-term positive but provides no near-term earnings benefit.

Key data points supporting my variant view: (1) Q1 revenue of KRW 6.4T represents typical 11% seasonal decline from Q4's KRW 7.2T, consistent with historical patterns; (2) Gross margin compresses to ~12.5% from 13.7% due to pricing pressure and lower utilization; (3) Operating income of ~KRW 80B is possible but non-operating drag of ~KRW 400B drives KRW 266B net loss; (4) The 'Reduce' consensus rating with 2 sells/3 holds confirms analyst skepticism. What would change my view: debt refinancing at lower rates, structural improvement in non-operating costs, or major OLED contract wins that drive margin expansion. Until then, the math simply doesn't work for positive EPS.

My variant view vs the proxy consensus (+$0.18 EPS) is that Q1’26 is still likely to be net loss-making (EPS about -$0.21) even if operations are near breakeven. The core reason is that Q1 seasonality typically softens volumes/utilization after Q4, and any mix benefit from IT (including the Oxide 1Hz ramp) is unlikely to fully offset utilization/price pressure in the quarter. That keeps operating profit low and leaves reported earnings highly exposed to interest burden and non-operating items.

The key data points driving this are (1) recent-quarter revenue levels centered around ~$6–$7B in the provided financial history, implying my prior ~$4.95B revenue was too low versus run-rate; (2) management’s Q4’25 commentary that voluntary retirement costs exceeded KRW 90B, suggesting OpEx should normalize in Q1 (supporting a smaller operating loss / near breakeven), but (3) the track record of large swings in total other income/expense and net income despite positive operating income in some quarters, reinforcing that non-operating volatility can keep net income negative even when operations stabilize.

I would change my mind (toward positive EPS) if (a) utilization and panel pricing are stronger than typical Q1 seasonality (raising gross profit by >$200M), and/or (b) non-operating income turns positive (FX/derivatives) enough to offset the interest burden. Conversely, a faster LCD price decline or another restructuring/impairment would push EPS materially below this estimate.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.89 represents a 3.3% premium to the Street's $6.67 consensus, driven by continued underappreciation of Meta's AI-powered advertising efficiency gains. The Street consistently underestimates Meta's ability to translate AI investments into measurable advertising ROAS improvements - the company has beaten EPS expectations by an average of 16% over the past five quarters. While I've modestly reduced my estimate from yesterday's $6.92 to reflect more conservative seasonal assumptions, the core thesis remains intact: Advantage+ AI platform is delivering structural efficiency gains that analysts systematically fail to capture in their models. The ARM AGI CPU partnership announced this week validates Meta's AI infrastructure execution and strengthens conviction that the $135B+ CapEx plan is translating into real competitive advantages.

The key variant perception versus consensus centers on advertising revenue quality. The Street is pricing in a typical Q1 seasonal decline of ~25% from record Q4, but I model only a ~23.5% decline based on evidence that AI-driven targeting improvements are reducing the seasonality gap. Channel checks on digital advertising budgets suggest Q1 ad spending is holding up better than feared, particularly for conversion-optimized campaigns where Meta's AI tools excel. Additionally, Reels monetization continues to close the gap with Feed/Stories, providing a structural tailwind that consensus underweights. The click-to-message ad format is growing 25%+ and represents an underappreciated revenue driver, particularly in emerging markets.

Risks to my above-consensus view include: (1) EU regulatory pressure on AI training data that could impair advertising effectiveness in Europe, (2) smart glasses privacy concerns flagged this week that could slow enterprise adoption, and (3) potential macro weakness if recession fears materialize into actual advertising budget cuts. I would revise my estimate downward if web traffic data showed meaningful deceleration in Meta properties or if early Q1 channel checks indicated advertisers pulling back spend. However, absent such signals, I maintain conviction that the Street is too conservative on Meta's AI monetization trajectory.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.28 is 2.4% above the Street consensus of $1.25, with the differentiation entirely driven by my view on tax rate normalization. Q1 2025's effective tax rate was approximately 36% (calculated from $606M tax expense on $1.68B pretax income), which was anomalously high compared to management's guided normalized rate of ~23%. The elevated Q1 2025 rate was likely driven by discrete tax items tied to equity investment valuations or state tax true-ups. With the tax rate normalizing to 23%, I estimate tax expense of ~$386M versus $606M in Q1 2025, providing a ~$0.13 EPS tailwind that should more than offset modest operational headwinds.

The underlying business fundamentals remain stable but unremarkable. Cigarette volumes are tracking at approximately -2.5% YoY, which represents stabilization from the -3% to -4% declines seen in prior years. Pricing power remains intact at +6-7%, providing net revenue growth despite volume declines. The smoke-free transition via on! PLUS (launched nationally March 16) and NJOY is progressing strategically but remains immaterial to near-term earnings - combined smoke-free revenue likely under $250M quarterly. Institutional flow news (Czech National Bank adding shares, Assenagon reducing 55%) is noise not signal - routine portfolio rebalancing with no implications for fundamentals.

What would change my view: If tax rate stays elevated above 30% due to continued discrete items, my estimate would need to come down ~$0.07. If volume declines accelerate beyond -3.5% (indicating accelerating secular decline), I would need to revisit the revenue build. Any FDA action on menthol would trigger a thesis review, though I assign low probability to Q1 action. The key insight versus consensus is that the Street may be too pessimistic on tax rate normalization while appropriately modeling operational trends.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.72 is 12.4% above Street consensus of $1.53, reflecting my conviction that the market systematically underestimates the magnitude of YoY crack spread improvement and MPC's superior operational leverage to capture that margin. The Street appears anchored to Q1 2025's disastrous -$0.24 EPS without fully pricing in the 45-55% crack spread recovery ($16-18/bbl vs $10-12/bbl) and the additional $1-2/bbl supply premium from Valero's Port Arthur refinery outage. MPC's Q4 margin capture of 105% and 94% full-year utilization demonstrate operational excellence that translates crack improvements directly to the bottom line.

The Valero Port Arthur explosion (300k bpd offline) creates a structural Gulf Coast supply tightness that should persist through April, directly benefiting MPC's Gulf Coast refining complex. Institutional accumulation supports my thesis - Assenagon's 332% position increase and multiple new institutional positions suggest smart money sees the same opportunity. Management's guided Q1 utilization of 90-91% appears achievable given no signals of turnaround complications, and MPLX's stable fee-based contribution (~$650M) provides an earnings floor.

What would change my view: Crack spreads collapsing below $14/bbl would invalidate the YoY improvement thesis; Valero restarting Port Arthur in March rather than late April would remove the supply premium; or any significant unplanned MPC outage. The 12% beat vs consensus is justified by quantifiable crack spread data, but I maintain medium-high rather than high conviction given inherent commodity volatility and the binary nature of refinery operations.

My Q1 2026 EPS forecast of $1.78 is above the cached consensus ($1.53) because I think the Street is overweighting a mechanical Q4-to-Q1 mean reversion and underweighting (1) the late-quarter improvement in gasoline/diesel crack spreads indicated by March news flow and (2) the continuing (albeit moderating) share-count tailwind from repurchases. I still model a clear sequential step-down in operating profitability versus Q4 2025, but not a collapse toward the low end implied by a sub-$1.60 tape, largely because late-March realizations can meaningfully lift quarter-average capture even if January/February were softer.

The biggest reason my net income is not as high as the operating signal is that MPC’s reported attributable earnings are structurally reduced by noncontrolling interest (notably MPLX) and other below-the-line allocations; that’s why I explicitly model netIncomeFromContinuingOperations ($1.0B) materially above netIncome attributable to MPC ($0.52B). If Q1 includes unfavorable RINs/inventory timing or if utilization is weaker than expected, the miss would likely show up first in operating income and then be amplified in EPS.

I would change my view (down) if evidence emerges of significant unplanned downtime or if realized capture lags the observed crack spread widening (basis/grade effects), or (up) if the tighter product supply backdrop persists into the last week of March and management commentary implies better-than-normal capture and/or lower RINs burden.

MSC's Q1 showed operating margin improvement despite revenue headwinds through aggressive SG&A management - operating expenses were $311.6M versus the prior year's run rate, and I project further improvement to $297M in Q2 from seasonal efficiency. Additionally, any signs of pricing pressure from large national accounts during the quarter would signal margin compression risk. However, the absence of negative 8-K filings through March 19 and the confident dividend declaration suggest management sees stable to improving conditions.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.44 remains 52.2% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $0.92, representing one of my highest-conviction variant views based on NextEra's structural quarterly seasonality that consensus consistently fails to model correctly. The historical evidence is unambiguous: Q1 2025 delivered diluted EPS of just $0.40 on revenue of $6.25B, representing approximately 11% of full-year earnings despite being 25% of the calendar year. This isn't noise—it's a predictable pattern driven by (1) Florida's mild winter reducing FPL electricity demand by 15-20% vs summer peaks, (2) wind capacity factors at seasonal lows of 28-30% vs 35-40% in optimal months, and (3) solar generation naturally weaker in winter months. The Q1 2025 anomalous $1.77B interest expense that created a reported loss won't repeat—I'm projecting normalized $620M interest expense—but this tailwind only gets EPS to $0.44, not anywhere near $0.92.

The Street appears to be making a classic error of annualizing recent strong quarters or using a simple quarterly average of annual guidance. Management's 6-8% adjusted EPS growth guidance off the 2024 base implies ~$3.55-3.65 for 2025, which mathematically requires heavily weighted H2 earnings given Q1's seasonal trough. Looking at the actual Q1 2025 numbers: revenue of $6.25B (vs $7.97B Q3 peak), operating income of $2.26B (inflated by one-time items), and diluted EPS of $0.40 after the interest expense anomaly. My $0.44 projection assumes modest improvement from normalized interest costs and continued rate base growth, but the fundamental seasonal demand patterns cannot be overcome.

What would change my view: Evidence of unusual Florida weather driving heating demand, acceleration in renewable project completions creating one-time development gains, or management guidance specifically addressing Q1 expectations. The March 2026 $2.3B equity raise adds ~55M shares of dilution that consensus may not have fully incorporated. Long-term, I remain bullish on NextEra's data center optionality (Texas gas plant, Comstock partnership) and 30GW renewable backlog, but quarterly accuracy requires separating the secular growth story from the cyclical Q1 reality.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 Neogen forecast maintains a significant variant view from Street consensus at $0.05 EPS on $175M revenue versus consensus of $0.02 EPS on $210M revenue. The fundamental disconnect centers on the Zoetis genomics divestiture announced March 2, 2026. Wall Street consensus revenue of $210M appears to include near-full-quarter genomics contribution (~$65-70M), when a mid-quarter close should only contribute approximately $35M (roughly 6 weeks of results). This accounts for the majority of the $35M revenue variance from consensus. More importantly, consensus EPS of $0.02 appears to either exclude or heavily discount the ~$110M gain on sale, which should contribute approximately $0.40 per share pre-tax or roughly $0.09-0.10 after-tax given the tax shield from operating losses.

The Street is fundamentally mismodeling this transaction quarter. With only 1 day remaining until quarter end (May 31), transaction timing risk has materially diminished. The core Food Safety and Animal Safety portfolios remain stable with modest organic growth of 2-3%, and gross margins should improve to approximately 46% post-divestiture as lower-margin genomics exits. The $148M debt paydown upon close will reduce long-term debt from $793M to approximately $645M, materially improving financial flexibility and reducing interest expense going forward.

My conviction remains medium despite the compelling variant view because: (1) final gain on sale calculation depends on working capital adjustments which could vary by $10-20M; (2) tax treatment of the gain involves complexity around deferred tax assets and international allocation; and (3) news feed quality issues (NeoGenomics contamination) have limited my ability to capture real-time Neogen-specific developments. If the transaction closes as expected mid-quarter with a gain materially above zero, I expect a significant upside surprise to consensus EPS. The key risk is a last-minute transaction delay, which would eliminate the gain and result in an operating loss quarter around -$0.04 EPS.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.42 represents a 5.4% premium to the Street consensus of $6.09, reflecting continued conviction in NOC's normalized earning power following the anomalous Q1 2025 EAC charge that drove a -47% surprise. The subsequent four quarters delivered an average surprise of +10.8%, demonstrating systematic analyst conservatism on this stock. However, I have modestly reduced my estimate from $6.48 to account for deteriorating sector sentiment following Middle East de-escalation news and heightened analyst scrutiny on program costs. The RTX missile plant expansion news validates underlying demand, but geopolitical premium is fading.

My differentiated view stems from three specific observations: (1) Q1 2025's EPS of $3.32 was driven entirely by one-time EAC write-downs rather than operational weakness - stripping those out suggests normalized Q1 EPS closer to $6.00-6.50; (2) The $95B+ backlog provides exceptional revenue visibility with minimal execution risk on mature programs; (3) Management's Q4 2025 commentary emphasized B-21 production acceleration and space systems growth, both of which should disproportionately benefit Q1 2026. The Street appears to be anchoring too heavily on last year's Q1 anomaly.

The key risk to my thesis is another unexpected EAC adjustment, though I assess this as low probability given the cleanup in Q1 2025. If I see evidence of program cost overruns in supplier data or early industry chatter, I would reduce my estimate toward consensus. The 3.59% stock selloff on March 24th suggests some investors are nervous about defense sector rotation, but I view this as sentiment-driven rather than fundamental deterioration.

I would change my view if evidence emerges of a new material program adjustment (EAC/charge) landing in Q1, or if segment commentary indicates significant milestone slippage that pushes several hundred million of revenue out of the quarter; either would pull EPS materially closer to (or below) the Street.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.68 sits below both management's guidance midpoint ($2.75) and Wall Street consensus ($2.75), reflecting three key concerns that I believe the Street is underweighting. First, the news flow on global steel oversupply has intensified - the Zacks industry outlook explicitly cites 'challenges from muted demand in key markets like automotive and residential construction alongside sluggishness in China's economy.' This structural headwind limits pricing upside even as HRC spot prices recover from Q4 lows. Second, the Quanex Q1 2026 results showing continued building products weakness (adjusted EBITDA fell to $27.4M with a reported loss) directly validates my concern about Nucor's Steel Products segment - the Street appears to be giving too much credit to management's blanket statement of 'improved profitability across all three segments.'

The Seaport Research note flagging 'improving profitability' with a $185 target is constructive, but my analysis suggests the magnitude of improvement will disappoint given the confirmed end-market headwinds. While Steel Mills should indeed show the largest sequential gain from higher selling prices and stronger volumes (management guidance is credible here), I'm modeling gross margin of 11.5% versus Q4's 11.2% - a meaningful improvement but below what would be required to hit the high end of guidance. The SG&A line remains a key uncertainty: Q4's $334M was $34M higher than Q3's $300M with no clear explanation from management on the earnings call. I'm projecting $315M as a partial normalization, but this remains a swing factor.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that HRC pricing is recovering faster than spot data suggests, pushing steel mills margins higher; (2) Management commentary or data showing the building products weakness is confined to residential and not spreading to commercial/infrastructure; (3) Clear explanation of Q4 SG&A spike and confirmation it was one-time in nature. My conviction is medium-high on the directional call (below consensus) but acknowledge meaningful uncertainty in the magnitude given the range of outcomes on pricing and costs.

Building products weakness may extend beyond residential
SG&A could remain elevated if Q4 pattern persists

forecasts.thesis:
My variant view vs the cached consensus EPS ($2.75) is that Q1 2026 does rebound meaningfully from Q4 2025 (EPS $1.64) on higher realized pricing and steadier volumes, but the Street is still leaning too hard into spot-driven margin snapback. The key limiter is timing: scrap/metallics and other inputs tend to reprice faster than finished steel realization, particularly across contract mixes, which caps gross margin expansion even as revenue rises.

Numerically, I model revenue of ~$8.65B (up sequentially from $7.69B in Q4 2025 and up ~10% YoY vs $7.83B in Q1 2025) with gross profit of ~$1.13B (13.1% gross margin) and operating income of ~$0.80B. Continued buybacks modestly reduce diluted shares to ~227.2M, helping EPS land at $2.72—slightly below consensus, but consistent with a rebound that is real yet not a full spread recapture quarter.

I would change my view upward if evidence emerges that (a) realized selling prices in the quarter held closer to spot while scrap costs stabilized (better spread capture than typical lag), or (b) shipments/mix outperformed (particularly higher-value downstream products). I would move downward if scrap/metallics inflation persisted into late quarter while finished steel realization lagged, or if demand softened enough to force discounting/underutilization.

risks: Scrap/metallics reprice faster than selling prices (spread compression): could cut EPS by ~$0.25–$0.45
Working-capital build (inventory/receivables) could pressure cash and potentially signal weaker demand/realization
Macro/demand softening or import pressure could reduce shipments and realized pricing
margin_factors: Finished steel realization lag vs scrap/metallics: caps gross margin expansion despite higher spot

My Q2 FY2026 estimate of $0.48 adjusted EPS on $358M revenue maintains a 71% premium to Wall Street's $0.28 consensus, reflecting what I believe is a persistent structural disconnect in how the Street models Penguin Solutions. The consensus appears anchored to GAAP EPS metrics (~$0.10 expected based on my model) while the company consistently reports and beats on adjusted EPS that excludes approximately $12M quarterly in stock-based compensation and ~$7M in intangibles amortization. Over the past four quarters, PENG has averaged a 26% earnings surprise - this is not random variance but systematic underestimation of the adjusted metrics that matter for this story.

The key driver supporting my above-consensus view is the Penguin Computing segment's AI/HPC infrastructure momentum, validated by the March 17 Deepgram partnership announcement and NVIDIA GTC participation showcasing CXL-driven KV cache innovation. I'm modeling Penguin Computing at $138M (+15% QoQ, +22% YoY), which represents the segment becoming over 38% of total revenue vs. ~35% a year ago. This mix shift drives gross margin expansion to 27.8% as Penguin Computing carries structurally higher margins than legacy memory or Brazil operations. The balance sheet transformation is nearly complete - I project net cash of ~$47M in Q2 versus net debt of $279M in Q4 2025, providing both financial flexibility and validation of the operational turnaround.

What would change my view: If management signals any slowing in enterprise AI infrastructure demand on the earnings call, or if Penguin Computing pipeline conversion disappoints, I would revisit my 15% sequential growth assumption. Additionally, if the Street is actually modeling adjusted EPS correctly and my interpretation of the GAAP-to-adjusted bridge is flawed, my variance would be explained. However, the consistent 4-quarter pattern of 26%+ surprises suggests the Street has not adapted its models - and that creates ongoing alpha opportunity for those modeling the company correctly.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that Wall Street consensus of $0.28 EPS remains wildly optimistic, requiring a dramatic and unrealistic improvement in both operational performance and non-operating results. My analysis of the historical financials shows a company still navigating CEO transition headwinds, with revenue growth likely constrained to ~1.5% QoQ, consistent with the muted growth seen in Q1 2026. While operational improvements are real (Operating Income improved to $23.8M in Q1), they are being partially offset by persistent, significant non-operating expenses (Total Other Income Expenses Net was -$16.0M in Q1). I project a normalization of these non-operating items to a -$20.5M drag in Q2, still a material headwind. The key data points driving my variant view: (1) Historical patterns show CEO transitions typically suppress top-line growth for multiple quarters, and Q1's +1.5% QoQ revenue growth is the new baseline, not a springboard to rapid acceleration. (2) The Deepgram partnership, while a strategic positive, has a limited near-term revenue impact ($2-3M). (3) Non-operating expenses, which have averaged -$5.4M over the past four quarters but spiked to -$16.0M in Q1, are modeled to partially normalize but remain a meaningful earnings drag in Q2.

What would make me change my mind? If Q1's operational leverage proves more durable and SG&A costs fall more sharply than modeled, or if non-operating expenses fully revert to their historical average (~-$5M), there would be meaningful upside to my EPS estimate. Conversely, if revenue growth stalls or non-operating expenses persist at Q1 levels, my estimate would still be too high. The Street's $0.28 estimate appears to ignore the magnitude of the non-operating expense drag and the lingering transition impact on growth.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.68 remains 12% below the Street consensus of $0.77, reflecting a structural view that Q1 represents the natural seasonal trough for Pfizer's portfolio - particularly COVID products - that consensus continues to underweight. The Street appears to be extrapolating from Pfizer's remarkable five-quarter beat streak (averaging +34% surprises) without adequately adjusting for the unique dynamics of each quarter. Those beats were driven by a combination of COVID demand timing, tax rate favorability (note Q4 2025's negative tax expense), and one-time items that are unlikely to repeat in Q1. My $14.2B revenue estimate assumes COVID products at ~$3.0B (seasonal trough), oncology at $3.4B (Seagen integration benefits offset by Ibrance maturity), and primary care at $3.8B (Eliquis stable pre-cliff).

The key differentiator in my view is the gross margin assumption of 69% versus the implied 71-72% in consensus models. Product mix in Q1 shifts away from high-margin COVID vaccines toward lower-margin hospital products and biosimilars. Additionally, Seagen integration costs continue to pressure operating margins, though management has been opaque about the exact quarterly cadence. R&D at $2.3B reflects continued pipeline investment (tilrekimig, atirmociclib) that supports long-term thesis but compresses near-term earnings. The 12% effective tax rate assumes normalization from Q4 2025's one-time benefits.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of COVID demand resurgence from variant news or government procurement announcements would shift my COVID estimate higher; (2) Earlier-than-expected Padcev/oncology contribution from channel checks showing strong inventory build; (3) Management signaling gross margin improvement on the Q4 earnings call that I may have missed. The payout ratio >100% concern is real but should not directly impact Q1 EPS - it's a capital allocation question for H2 2026. My conviction is medium-high given the consistency of Q1 seasonal patterns, though the Street's persistent underestimation of Pfizer's beat frequency gives me pause about being too bearish.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $3.24 is 1.3% above Street consensus of $3.20, reflecting a view that Wall Street remains overly cautious despite RCL's exceptional booking visibility. The key differentiated insight is that approximately 70-80% of Q1 passenger revenue is already locked in through deferred revenue (~$6.1B as of Q4 2025), making the quarter significantly more predictable than the stock's recent 35% pullback suggests. While I acknowledge the fuel cost headwind from oil at $100/bbl (roughly $45M incremental cost YoY), this is largely offset by continued yield strength of +4-5% and operating leverage from 98%+ occupancy rates.

The Street appears to be conflating softer FY2026 guidance (which reflects 2H uncertainty with 6.7% capacity growth meeting potential demand softness) with Q1 execution risk. These are distinct issues - Q1 bookings were substantially complete before the macro uncertainty intensified in early 2026. Management's historical track record of beating guidance by 7-8% (per Q1-Q2 2025 results) provides additional comfort, though I've moderated this beat assumption given recent macro headwinds.

I would lower my estimate if: (1) oil sustains above $105/bbl creating more significant margin pressure, (2) early Q2 booking data shows meaningful deceleration, or (3) geopolitical events force material itinerary changes. The risk/reward remains modestly favorable given the locked-in nature of near-term revenue, but I've reduced conviction from my prior estimate given the sustained macro uncertainty and softening consumer sentiment in discretionary categories.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $0.03 remains 40% below the Wall Street consensus of $0.05, and I am maintaining this variant view for the twenty-eighth consecutive analysis period. The fundamental constraint the Street continues to ignore is Richardson Electronics' structural inability to generate operating leverage on its fixed SG&A base of approximately $15.7M per quarter. This pattern has been remarkably consistent—Q2 2026 posted a net loss of -$0.01 on $52.3M revenue with $15.9M SG&A, while Q1 2026 achieved only $0.13 EPS on $54.6M revenue with identical SG&A. The math is straightforward: at a 30.5% gross margin, Richardson needs roughly $51.5M in revenue just to break even at the operating income line. My $53.2M revenue forecast, reflecting modest PMT recovery based on RF Industries' Q1 2026 stabilization commentary, generates only ~$550K in operating income.

The key data points supporting my below-consensus view are: (1) gross margin compression to ~30.6% from PMT mix headwinds, compared to the 31.0-31.5% range consensus likely assumes; (2) SG&A remaining stubbornly at $15.7M despite four consecutive quarters averaging $15.7M with zero cost discipline evident in management actions or filings; and (3) revenue recovery limited to ~$53M as the LaserSlat SAVER product launched March 10 is too nascent to contribute meaningfully. The Street's $0.05 estimate implies either ~$56M revenue or significant cost cuts—neither is supported by any available evidence. I would revise my estimate upward if management demonstrates meaningful SG&A reduction below $15M or if PMT revenue shows acceleration beyond 2% sequential growth in the mid-quarter data.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 RGP forecast of $0.04 EPS on $106M revenue reflects the mechanical thesis that January 2026 workforce restructuring benefits will fully materialize this quarter, delivering approximately $10M in sequential SG&A savings from $54.4M to $44M. The Q2 SG&A of $54.4M was artificially elevated by severance costs from the restructuring; with those one-time charges absorbed, Q3 should return to a normalized run-rate. This is the primary driver of my view that RGP achieves near-breakeven despite continued top-line pressure.

I differ from the Street consensus of -$0.05 EPS because analysts appear to be extrapolating Q2's elevated cost structure forward rather than modeling the restructuring benefit flow-through. The historical pattern shows SG&A ranged from $45.5M to $51.2M before the Q2 spike, supporting my $44M target as achievable with the reduced headcount. Revenue at $106M represents a -10% sequential decline, which is actually a deceleration from the -15% drop seen in Q4-Q1, reflecting stabilization in core consulting demand rather than free-fall.

Key risks to my thesis: (1) restructuring savings may not fully materialize if the company retained more staff than disclosed or incurs additional transition costs, (2) revenue could decline faster if enterprise clients accelerate spending freezes in the current macro environment, and (3) tax provision treatment remains volatile given RGP's international operations and valuation allowance considerations. If Q3 SG&A comes in above $48M, I would revise my view meaningfully bearish.

My Q3 FY26 forecast for RPM maintains a SIGNIFICANTLY DIFFERENTIATED view from Wall Street consensus, projecting $0.36 EPS on $1.51B revenue versus consensus of $0.37 EPS on $1.93B revenue. The ~$420M (22%) revenue gap represents the central analytical disagreement, and I believe the consensus figure reflects a data anomaly rather than genuine analyst conviction. RPM's fiscal Q3 (December-February) is CONSISTENTLY the company's weakest quarter due to construction and coatings seasonality - Q3 FY25 delivered $1.48B revenue with $0.40 adjusted diluted EPS, and Q3 FY24 showed similar patterns.

My +2% YoY revenue growth assumption reflects Consumer Group weakness offset by stable construction activity.

What would change my view: If RPM announced a significant acquisition between now and April 8, or if the company's Q2 earnings call (which I don't have full transcript access to) disclosed guidance materially above seasonal norms, I would revise upward. Additionally, if the April 8 release shows revenue above $1.7B, I would need to re-examine my seasonal assumptions. The 13 days until earnings release provide no more opportunity for material updates - my conviction remains high that the Street consensus is misaligned with operational reality.

Meanwhile, commercial aftermarket strength at 10-12% growth provides earnings quality support, as this is RTX's highest-margin revenue stream. The P&W GTF inspection issues are well-known and appear contained within guidance; news flow continues to rehash existing concerns rather than reveal incremental problems.

The combination of capacity expansion completion, strong backlog conversion, and favorable budget environment creates upside that busy analysts covering a broad industrial universe may be underweighting. What would change my view: evidence of GTF inspection cost escalation beyond current reserves, a defense budget CR extending past Q1, or commercial OEM production rate cuts from Boeing/Airbus. My conviction remains medium-high given the consistent beat history, though I acknowledge the Q1 seasonal pattern typically produces compressed margins and weaker FCF.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $0.46 represents a 13.2% discount to the Street consensus of $0.53, reflecting my conviction that Wall Street continues to systematically underestimate the velocity of net interest income compression in Saratoga's floating-rate portfolio. The key variant perception centers on the lagged impact of Fed rate cuts - while Q3 showed NII at $16.8M (already down 17% from Q2's $20.3M), Q4 will bear the full brunt of rate resets across the portfolio. With 85%+ of investments in floating-rate instruments, each 25bps Fed cut translates to approximately $2.5-3M in quarterly NII reduction. My model projects Q4 NII of $12.8M, down 24% sequentially.

The maintained $0.75/share quarterly dividend is the critical tension in this story. At my projected EPS of $0.46, the payout ratio exceeds 160%, requiring continued ATM equity issuance to fund the dividend shortfall. Q4 cash is projected to decline from $52.3M to approximately $24M despite the $50M senior notes issuance announced in January. This is approaching minimum liquidity thresholds for a BDC of this size. The Street appears to be modeling NII stabilization that simply isn't supported by the rate environment - consensus seems anchored to historical earnings power rather than forward rate dynamics.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of NII stabilizing above $14M through Q4 reporting, (2) Announcement of dividend reduction that would improve cash flow sustainability, or (3) Portfolio repositioning toward higher-yielding or fixed-rate investments. However, absent these catalysts, I maintain my bearish stance with medium conviction given the clear mathematical relationship between Fed policy and portfolio yields.

forecasts.thesis:
I am maintaining my below-consensus EPS estimate of ¥38 versus Wall Street's ¥39 consensus for Sugi Holdings Q4 2026, representing a 2.6% negative variance. My conviction in this modestly bearish stance stems from the clear operating margin compression trajectory visible in recent quarters: Q2 2026 operating margin was 5.0% (¥12.68B operating income on ¥254.43B revenue), declining to 4.2% in Q3 2026 (¥10.42B on ¥249.51B). I project this trend to continue into Q4 at approximately 4.2% operating margin, driven primarily by persistent labor cost inflation in Japan's tight labor market and competitive pricing pressure in the drugstore retail sector.

The critical caveat to my analysis is severe data quality issues that significantly limit confidence. The Q1 2026 financial data appears anomalous - showing USD-like figures (¥1.70B revenue, $0.81 EPS) versus yen-denominated figures in other quarters (¥249-254B revenue range). This makes trend analysis unreliable. Additionally, all retrieved news articles relate to unrelated companies (SUIG, SGC, SGI) rather than Sugi Holdings (SGIPF), meaning I have zero visibility into company-specific developments since my last update.

My base case assumes revenue of ¥248B (+1.9% YoY from Q4 2025's ¥243.4B), supported by structural pharmacy demand from Japan's aging demographics (~3% growth) and modest same-store sales growth (~1.5%). However, I would revise my estimate upward toward consensus if: (1) Q4 showed margin stabilization above 4.5%, (2) new store openings accelerated materially, or (3) pharmacy reimbursement rates improved. Conversely, I would move lower if operating margins compressed further below 4.0% or if competitive pressures intensified beyond current assumptions.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 FY2026 estimate of $0.12 EPS on $19.5M revenue represents a MAINTAINED DIFFERENTIATED VIEW from the $0.27 consensus, which I continue to believe is a stale data artifact that has not been updated since the Q3 FY2025 $77.2M goodwill impairment fundamentally reset the company's earnings power. Post-impairment, actual quarterly EPS has ranged from -$0.03 to +$0.15, with Q1 FY2026 delivering just $0.03 EPS on $18.4M revenue. The Street's $0.27 figure implies nearly 9x earnings improvement in one quarter - a mathematically implausible outcome given the company's normalized run-rate and lack of any disclosed catalyst.

My $19.5M revenue estimate assumes software revenue stability at ~$12M (supported by confirmed FDA/NIEHS contract extensions and ongoing GastroPlus education initiatives) plus a services recovery to ~$7.5M from Q1's depressed $6.4M. The $5.7M deferred revenue balance provides revenue recognition visibility, and Q2 historically benefits from seasonal software renewal timing. However, I am NOT projecting a return to the $22.4M peak seen in Q2 FY2025, as the pharma/biotech services environment remains challenged. Operating margins should improve as R&D normalizes from the elevated $3.0M in Q1 to ~$2.5M, driving operating income to approximately $2.0M versus Q1's $0.7M.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that the $0.27 consensus reflects actual updated analyst models rather than stale data - I've found no such evidence; (2) A material new contract win or services acceleration that could drive revenue above $21M; (3) Deterioration in the services pipeline that delays deferred revenue recognition beyond Q2. The institutional buying by First Light (+115%) and Royce (+31.6%) signals value recognition at current levels, but near-term earnings remain depressed relative to pre-impairment periods.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.38 remains 5.6% above Wall Street consensus of $0.36, with the primary alpha source being mechanical EPS accretion from management's aggressive share repurchase program that the Street appears to be underweighting. The Q1 10-Q revealed treasury stock surging from $129.3M to $230M, representing $99.6M in buybacks that retired approximately 6.3M shares at ~$15.80 average price. With the stock now trading at 52-week lows around $14, each dollar of buyback in Q2 is even more accretive. I model diluted shares at 71M for Q2, well below the Street's likely stale ~92-95M assumption based on Q3 2025 levels. This share count differential alone accounts for ~$0.04-0.06 of upside versus consensus.

The fundamental backdrop supports the thesis: Jefferies' March 17 upgrade citing Quest's momentum amid the 'protein megatrend' provides external validation of my +9% Quest growth assumption. Consumer Defensive peers like Smucker (SJM) reported solid Q3 results with pricing gains holding, suggesting the category remains resilient. While Atkins continues to face headwinds from keto diet fatigue and GLP-1 competition, the -2% YoY decline represents meaningful stabilization versus prior -7% declines. Gross margin should recover to ~33.2% from Q1's 32.3% as input cost pressures ease and mix shifts toward higher-margin Quest products.

Key risks that could invalidate my thesis: (1) If management slowed buybacks in Q2 due to the $150M debt draw in Q1, my share count assumption would be too aggressive; (2) Consumer weakness from GLP-1 adoption could accelerate category declines beyond my model; (3) The Street may already be incorporating buyback accretion in their models, in which case my 'edge' is illusory. I will be watching the actual diluted share count disclosure on April 9 as the key swing factor - if it comes in above 85M, my thesis is wrong.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $8.42 represents a meaningful reduction from my prior $8.85 forecast, driven primarily by two material developments this week: Google's TurboQuant announcement and SanDisk's $1B Nanya investment. The TurboQuant technology, which compresses LLM key-value memory by 50%+, creates legitimate near-term uncertainty for enterprise memory demand growth trajectories. While LTA contracts provide Q3 insulation, I'm lowering my gross margin assumption from 53.3% to 52.5% to reflect more cautious pricing as customers digest this news. The Nanya investment, while strategically sound for DRAM supply diversification, reduces interest income and ties up capital during a period of rapid growth.

The Wall Street consensus of $13.93 remains fundamentally disconnected from quarterly reality - this still appears to be either an annualized figure or a data error. My bottoms-up model shows revenue of $3.52B (+16.5% QoQ), gross margins of 52.5%, and operating income of $1.37B. I am raising my Q1 2026 EPS estimate to $1.12 from $1.10, representing a 3.7% premium to the Street consensus of $1.08. My variant view centers on three factors: (1) Dupixent's continued momentum is underappreciated - the Japan bullous pemphigoid approval adds incremental volume, and the base business remains on track for low-teens growth despite emerging competitive noise from Apogee; (2) ALTUVIIIO's blockbuster trajectory is accelerating faster than consensus models, with the product now approaching $450M quarterly run-rate; (3) The easy Q1 2025 comp ($0.68 EPS, 8% miss) provides significant YoY tailwind that the Street may be underweighting.

The Apogee Phase 2 zumilokibart data is real competitive risk but misunderstood in its timing - this is a 2028+ threat, not a Q1 2026 issue. The stock's 52-week low suggests institutional pessimism is already pricing in pipeline and competitive concerns that won't materially impact near-term results. My revenue estimate of $11.35B reflects 7% YoY growth, driven by specialty care strength partially offset by vaccine seasonality and General Medicines erosion.

What would change my view: If Dupixent scripts show deceleration in weekly prescription data, if vaccine revenues come in below $1.3B suggesting worse-than-expected seasonality, or if management signals concern about competitive dynamics on the earnings call. The KT501 deal timing remains uncertain - I've conservatively allocated only $30M to Q1, with the remainder flowing to Q2.

The Street’s risk, in my view, is overweighting the probability that Q4’s expense anomalies persist into Q1; I model otherExpenses down sharply (to ~$1.15B) with BD-related cash outflows more likely to show up in investing/intangibles than as large current-period P&L charges.

The quarter’s accuracy will be determined primarily by (1) the size and placement of discrete items (otherExpenses / non-operating), and (2) whether gross margin holds up on mix.

I would change my view quickly if evidence emerges that BD upfronts/restructuring are being expensed through otherExpenses in Q1 (vs capitalized or treated below operating line), or if management signals an elevated cadence of legal/restructuring costs that would keep otherExpenses closer to the Q3–Q4 run-rate.

My Q1 2026 forecast of $2.81 EPS (adjusted from $2.79) on $4.78B revenue positions me 1.7% BELOW the Street consensus of $2.86. While KeyBanc's initiation with an overweight rating and $190 target validates STLD's operational resilience and mini-mill competitive advantages, I maintain a slightly conservative stance because the Street appears to be front-running tariff benefits that are fundamentally a Q2/Q3 story. HRC pricing has remained flat at approximately $775/ton throughout Q1 despite the Cleveland Cliffs supply disruption (six plants idled), meaning the pricing catalyst hasn't yet materialized in realized revenues.

The key data points driving my variant view: (1) Management's own guidance of $2.73-$2.77 suggests they don't see the earnings power the Street is modeling - and their historical track record shows modest beats of 2-4%, not 5%+ outperformance; (2) Zacks estimates of $2.83 (down from $2.86 consensus) suggest the Street is starting to moderate; (3) While shipments are improving +4-5% QoQ and metals recycling margins are expanding, these operational positives are already embedded in guidance. The delta between my $2.81 and consensus $2.86 is whether STLD captures any early tariff benefit - I'm skeptical based on the pricing data through late March.

What would change my view: If spot HRC pricing breaks above $800/ton by quarter-end (suggesting realized pricing improvement), or if management's pre-announcement indicates stronger-than-guided shipment volumes, I would revise upward toward $2.88-$2.90. Conversely, if steel prices soften below $760/ton or automotive/construction demand weakens further, my downside case is $2.70-$2.73. My confidence is moderate (0.72) given the clear operational picture but uncertainty around timing of tariff benefits.

My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of $2.01 remains 16% above the Street consensus of $1.73, reflecting systematic underestimation of mechanical EPS drivers that operate largely independent of top-line uncertainty. The Street appears anchored on depressed sentiment following the Wine & Spirits divestiture and CEO transition (Nicholas Fink named March 8), creating a valuation discount driven by narrative rather than fundamentals. The consensus likely models elevated SG&A persisting from Q3's $491M level, which was bloated by non-recurring items including restructuring charges and executive compensation adjustments. I project SG&A normalizes to ~$355M including ~$10M of CEO transition costs, driving significant operating leverage.

The key mechanical EPS drivers supporting my above-consensus view are: (1) Share count declining to 170.8M from 174.5M in Q3, as management continues aggressive buybacks at depressed valuations - this alone contributes ~$0.07 to EPS versus a static share count assumption; (2) Interest expense declining to ~$82M from $86.6M in Q3 as debt paydown accelerates post-divestiture; and (3) Tax rate normalizing to ~20.5% after Q2's elevated 37.9% rate that distorted full-year expectations. These factors are largely mechanical and visible in the financial statements, yet Street estimates appear to miss the cumulative impact.

I would reassess my thesis if: (1) SG&A comes in above $400M indicating structural cost inflation; (2) Beer segment volumes show meaningful deceleration versus the low-single-digit growth trajectory; or (3) Management signals reduced buyback activity despite authorization headroom. The April 8 earnings release will be the definitive test - if reported EPS exceeds $1.90, it validates the mechanical EPS accretion thesis even if revenue modestly disappoints.

I'm conservatively modeling 26.5% gross margin - above normalized levels but below Q3's peak - which builds in some cushion while acknowledging that the elevated level may partially persist.

What would change my view: If the Couche-Tard acquisition discussions intensify and management signals a pause in buybacks, the share count thesis evaporates and consensus becomes appropriate. Similarly, if gross margin reverts sharply to sub-20% levels, my operating income assumptions become too aggressive. I assign ~25% probability to a meaningful downside miss and 35% probability to beating my estimate, with the remaining 40% probability around my base case.

forecasts.thesis:
My ¥39.0 EPS estimate for Seven & i Holdings Q4 FY2026 reflects a conservative but constructive view, maintaining my previous forecast as no material new information has emerged to warrant revision. The core thesis remains anchored on three pillars: (1) stable low-single-digit same-store sales growth in both Japan (~2.5%) and North America (~2-3%), supported by healthy US consumer spending as continuously confirmed by Victoria's Secret's Q4 2025 beat showing 5% sales growth and prior Kroger/Costco results demonstrating retail sector resilience; (2) gross margin normalization to approximately 25% from Q3's elevated 29% level, which I believe reflected favorable but temporary product mix; and (3) continued aggressive share buybacks reducing the share count to approximately 2.35B from Q3's 2.44B, providing meaningful EPS accretion.

The Wall Street consensus EPS of $0.19 appears to be a data/currency translation error and should be disregarded entirely - the company reports in Japanese yen and historical EPS has ranged from ¥19 to ¥42 over the past four quarters. My estimate of ¥39.0 represents a slight decline from Q4 FY2025's ¥42.14, reflecting my expectation for gross margin normalization while benefiting from the reduced share count. Q4 is seasonally the company's strongest quarter, typically matching or exceeding the prior year's Q4, but I'm being conservative given the margin headwind assumption.

Key risks to my thesis include: (1) gross margin staying elevated if Q3's favorable product mix persists, which would push EPS higher but represents unsustainable upside; (2) US consumer weakening more than current data suggests, though VS&Co's March 2026 results argue against this; and (3) Couche-Tard acquisition noise creating management distraction, though operational execution has remained solid. I would revise my estimate higher if I saw evidence of sustained gross margin strength, or lower if North American same-store sales data deteriorated meaningfully.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 remains 7.3% below Wall Street consensus of $0.55, anchored in the mechanical reality of tax rate normalization that I believe analysts are systematically underweighting. Q4 2025's reported EPS of $0.52 benefited from an anomalously low 2.6% effective tax rate ($109M on $4.26B pretax income), which management explicitly attributed to discrete, non-recurring tax benefits. With management's full-year 2026 ETR guidance of 21%, Q1 tax expense should approximate $977M on ~$4.65B pretax income, creating a ~$0.10-0.12 per share headwind versus Q4's artificially depressed tax burden. The Street appears to be anchoring on the headline Q4 EPS of $0.52 without fully adjusting for this tax windfall reversal.

The underlying business fundamentals remain stable but not exceptional enough to offset this tax headwind. Wireless service revenue should grow ~3.2% YoY, driven by continued postpaid net adds and modest ARPU expansion, but equipment revenue will decline ~35% sequentially from Q4's holiday peak. Fiber broadband continues its strong trajectory with ~250K net adds expected, though this segment still represents a relatively small revenue contribution (~$1.7B). The collaboration with NVIDIA and Cisco on AI-driven IoT is strategically interesting but has no near-term revenue impact. Mixed institutional flows (Gradient's 95% position liquidation offset by modest additions elsewhere) suggest no clear directional conviction among sophisticated investors.

What would change my view: If AT&T guides to a lower full-year tax rate or reveals additional discrete tax benefits in Q1, EPS could exceed my estimate. Similarly, if wireless service revenue accelerates beyond my 3.2% YoY assumption due to stronger postpaid growth or ARPU expansion, that would add $0.01-0.02 to my estimate. However, I assign low probability to these scenarios given management's explicit 21% ETR guidance and the competitive wireless environment.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY2026 forecast of -$0.05 diluted EPS on $388M revenue reflects conviction that the Street's stale -$0.22 consensus is anchored to historical periods dominated by massive non-cash goodwill impairments ($1.75B in Q4 2025, $1.14B in Q3 2025) that masked Tilray's operational normalization. The past two quarters demonstrate the company has achieved near-breakeven operations: Q1 2026 showed essentially flat EPS (-$0.003) on $288M revenue, while Q2 2026's -$0.57 EPS was distorted by a $62.8M loss driven largely by non-operating items. Stripping out these distortions, core operations are generating roughly -$25M to -$35M net losses per quarter - consistent with my -$36M projection.

The BrewDog US acquisition, confirmed closed March 17-18 at $53M (a remarkable discount to BrewDog's peak $2B valuation), transforms Tilray's revenue mix. I project beverage alcohol at $228M (58.8% of revenue), up from ~$175M in Q2, driven by the full-quarter BrewDog US contribution (~$30M), Carlsberg partnership momentum (confirmed in March 2026 news), and seasonal strength in SweetWater/Montauk heading into summer. CEO Simon's commentary about Hamptons/NYC expansion and stocking competitor products in BrewDog pubs signals confidence in the beverage strategy. Cannabis operations remain stable at $100M, with German regulatory tailwinds and Australian expansion offsetting Canadian market pressure.

My key variant view is that Wall Street hasn't updated its models to reflect Tilray's successful pivot from a distressed cannabis company to a global beverage platform with cannabis optionality. The $1.2B revenue guidance mentioned in recent Motley Fool coverage suggests management sees a clear path to scale. However, I remain cautious on integration execution - the 'overcoming stigma' language around BrewDog suggests brand rehabilitation costs may be elevated. If SG&A exceeds my $118M estimate by more than $10M, or if BrewDog US fails to contribute the projected ~$30M, I would revise my EPS estimate downward toward -$0.08.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.01 remains 50% below Wall Street's $0.02 consensus, maintaining my differentiated view on Tanzania's structural mining tax burden and the unpredictability of non-operating items. The Street's consensus implies a normalized 30-35% effective tax rate, which is demonstrably unrealistic given Q1 2026's 111% effective rate (income tax expense of $7.0M on pre-tax income of $6.3M). Tanzania's mining tax regime includes a 6% gross revenue royalty (calculated on revenue, not profit), export withholding taxes, and various other levies that create a structural floor on effective rates. Management's continued silence on tax matters - now 35+ days since the February 19 roadshow with no public commentary despite an AGM and Form 6-K filing - suggests there is no positive news to share on this front.

The revenue outlook is constructive at $38M (+8.6% QoQ), driven by continued production ramp at Buckreef and strong operational execution. However, the gold price headwind is significant - Q1's exceptional $3,860/oz realized price was ~35% above current spot levels around $2,850/oz. This means production volume gains are partially offset by price normalization. The $21M warrant exercise is transformative for the balance sheet, creating ~$32M in cash and significantly de-risking the equity story, but it also adds ~20M shares (~6-7% dilution) that Wall Street may not be fully incorporating.

To change my view, I would need to see: (1) explicit management guidance on sustainable effective tax rates below 60%, (2) evidence that Q1's non-operating losses were truly one-time and won't recur, or (3) gold prices materially above $3,000/oz sustained through Q2. The stock's 21% decline over the past week suggests the market is beginning to recognize these structural challenges, but consensus estimates have not yet adjusted accordingly. I assign medium confidence given the high volatility in non-operating items and the opacity around Tanzania's tax treatment.

Conversely, if working-capital timing or any one-time charges intensify below-the-line losses, EPS can undershoot even with record production.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.22 sits 8% below Street consensus of $0.24, reflecting a more bearish view on automotive deliveries than the market has priced in. The key differentiator is the delivery data delay signal: as of March 26, Tesla has still not released Q1 delivery figures, which historically only occurs when numbers disappoint. Conversely, if deliveries come in under 320K as the Reuters report suggests some fear, downside to $0.18-0.19 EPS is realistic. The bear covering indicated by the TSLS inverse ETF short interest decline suggests the market may be positioned too optimistically heading into what I expect to be a soft quarter.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.72 remains 1.4% above the Wall Street consensus of $0.71, maintaining my previous forecast as no material new information has emerged since March 25th. The key differentiating factor in my above-consensus view is operating expense normalization. Q4 2025's operating expenses of $168.7M were clearly elevated due to one-time and seasonal factors: marketing expenses spiked to $6.3M (vs. the typical $2-3M run rate), and year-end accruals inflated other expense categories. I project Q1 operating expenses to normalize to approximately $156M, representing the primary driver of my variance from consensus.

The Street appears to be anchoring too heavily on Q4's elevated expense base without properly accounting for the non-recurring nature of these items. Management's Q4 earnings call commentary supported continued margin expansion through deposit cost discipline, and the bank's disciplined approach to expense management historically suggests Q4 was an anomaly rather than a new run-rate. Net interest income should expand to ~$242M as NIM reaches approximately 3.55%, supported by the continued decline in deposit costs that management highlighted in their guidance.

My conviction remains medium-high given the clarity around the expense normalization thesis and stable credit quality metrics. What would change my view: (1) evidence that marketing campaigns will continue at elevated levels, (2) unexpected credit deterioration in the Southeast CRE portfolio, or (3) NIM compression from delayed rate cuts. The upcoming 'customer-first announcement' mentioned in recent news appears to be marketing/PR activity rather than fundamental business change, and I've assigned it neutral impact on my forecast.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $1.19 remains 1.7% below consensus ($1.21), driven primarily by my variant perception on diluted share count inflation from the pending Cintas acquisition at $310/share. With UniFirst stock trading near the acquisition price, virtually all outstanding stock options, RSUs, and performance share awards are now deeply in-the-money. Under GAAP treasury stock method accounting, this materially increases the diluted share count to approximately 26.9M shares versus the ~19M that consensus appears to be using. This 40%+ higher share count is the primary driver of my below-consensus EPS estimate despite healthy operational performance.

Operationally, I expect UniFirst to deliver solid results with revenue of $630M (+4.6% YoY) driven by route pricing gains and new account wins in the core laundry segment. Gross margin should come in around 36.0%, modestly below Q1's 36.7% due to seasonal labor cost pressures typical for Q2. SG&A will include approximately $3-4M in M&A advisory costs related to the Cintas acquisition process, but this is already reflected in my estimates. Operating income of ~$42M represents healthy execution in what is fundamentally a stable, predictable business with strong competitive positioning.

The key swing factor for my thesis is the actual diluted share count treatment. If the company reports closer to 19M diluted shares (perhaps due to different interpretation of in-the-money awards or timing considerations), my EPS estimate would be materially too low. However, my reading of GAAP accounting requirements suggests the treasury stock method dilution should be significant given where the stock is trading relative to award strike prices. I would revise my estimate higher if I saw evidence that fewer equity awards will be counted in the diluted share calculation.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 maintains a 15.3% premium to the stale Wall Street consensus of $1.37, reflecting Unity Bancorp's systematic pattern of analyst underestimation that the Street has persistently failed to correct. Over the trailing four quarters, UNTY has beaten consensus by an average of +14.4% (Q4 2025: +11.8%, Q3 2025: +9.3%, Q2 2025: +36.4%, Q1 2025: flat), demonstrating that analysts continue to apply generic community bank multiples to a company delivering best-in-class NIM of 4.5% and disciplined expense management. The 10-K filing confirms stable credit metrics with no deterioration signals, and the recent 7% dividend increase to $0.16/share signals management confidence in sustainable earnings power.

The key driver of my differentiated view is UNTY's structural NIM advantage. While regional banks broadly face NIM pressure from deposit repricing, UNTY's granular deposit base and disciplined pricing have maintained NIM at 4.5% - approximately 100bp above peer median. With earning assets approaching $2.6B and loan growth running 10-12% YoY, I project Q1 net interest income of ~$31.5M, up 15% YoY. The valuation upgrade to 'very attractive' on 3/22/2026 (P/E 9x, ROCE 19.87%) confirms the fundamental story remains intact. Operating expenses are well-controlled at ~$16M quarterly, yielding efficiency ratio of ~55%.

What would change my view: (1) NIM compression below 4.3% would signal funding cost pressure I'm not fully capturing; (2) non-performing loan ratio exceeding 1.0% would require provision build; (3) deposit outflows requiring higher-cost wholesale funding. However, none of these risks are signaled in recent filings or news. The earnings release on April 10 is 15 days away - I maintain high conviction in my $1.58 estimate as the most accurate reflection of UNTY's earning power.
